newsitem.title: USA: G7 to tackle terrorist fund-raising.
newsitem.headline: G7 to tackle terrorist fund-raising.

text.p: The Group of Seven top industrial democracies and Russia agreed Saturday to step up their fight against terrorism, including fund-raising by terrorists and potential attacks on computer systems.
"Our joint message to terrorists is this: you have nowhere to run and nowhere to hide," U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told reporters.

Counter-terrorism has been a theme of G7 summits for a decade but a statement issued here by foreign ministers of the eight countries participating in this year's meeting pledged to extend the struggle to new areas.

"To promote further cooperation, our governments will compare their domestic legislation related to terrorist fund-raising, and ensure strong domestic laws and controls over the manufacture, trading and transport of explosives," the ministers said.

In Denver, where the summit was held, former soldier Timothy McVeigh was sentenced to death last week for bombing an Oklahoma City federal building in 1995 and causing the deaths of 168 people in the worst mass murder in U.S. history.
Although the United States has been seen as a prime mover of measures against terrorism, the fund-raising issue is one that has exposed Washington itself to foreign criticism.

Britain has long complained that the Irish Republican Army has been able to raise money in the United States, and Israel has also been perturbed about fund-raising by the Hamas resistance movement, nominally for charitable purposes.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister Tony Blair discussed Northern Ireland in Denver earlier Saturday, but British officials said IRA fund-raising did not come up.

The ministers' statement said that to protect electronic and computer systems from disruption by terrorists, G7 countries would share information on ways of preventing attacks and preventing use of computer systems for terrorist purposes.

They also pledged to try to foil terrorist use of high explosives, sophisticated technology and "materials of mass destruction" and said a conference of experts would be held in Honolulu in September on security for international events.
On other issues, the ministers said experts would consider proposals for disrupting major transnational crime syndicates.
They said they had agreed on "practical extradition and mutual assistance measures" to help bring criminals to justice, but gave no details.
